reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: Thirty-five home runs and 30 steals from a shortstop is a rare combination, and the Statcast profile explains how it's happening without being a pure contact story. The power reads as legitimate at a 10.3% barrel rate with an .xSLG of .446, even though the 89.5 mph average exit velocity is right at the median, because he's generating barrels efficiently rather than just mashing everything hard. What makes him genuinely dangerous is that the projection's .273/.347/.511 line assumes his legs keep doing real work alongside the pop, and at 28.5 ft/s he has the speed to post 30 steals in a full season. The catch in the profile is the 37.2% chase rate, which is a real liability, and if pitchers learn to exploit it more aggressively the strikeouts climb past 23.2% and the walks stay stuck near 8.6%, which puts pressure on everything downstream.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .419 and the barrel rate is 20.8%, both maxing out the percentile chart, and the contact quality case for Wood is essentially closed. The problem is a 28.6% strikeout rate that sits near the bottom of the league, meaning a lot of that monster exit-velocity profile never reaches a box score. What saves it is an elite 16.8% walk rate: he earns enough free passes that the damage he does make contact on keeps the projection at .388 OBP and .527 SLG, a genuine middle-of-the-order line at 23. If pitchers find a repeatable pattern in that 30.7% whiff rate and strikeouts climb further, the counting stats soften, but 95.1 mph average exit velocity is the kind of foundation that survives some swing-and-miss.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.
reports.report: Hitters have to earn their way on, and he can finish them; nothing in the line points to a weakness yet; the next level is the real test. Current-performance ceiling scenario: mid-rotation starter; the sample covers 93.3 IP in Double-A, so confidence is moderate.

If the command holds even at its current level, you're looking at a front-of-rotation arm for a long time.

reports.name: Liam Doyle
reports.published_report: The strikeout stuff is legitimate, the walk rate is the whole argument. Doyle is running 11.9 K/9 across 87 innings at AA, which translates to 9.3 per nine in MLB terms — strikeouts travel well through the level adjustment. The problem is 49 walks in those same 87 innings, a 5.1 BB/9 that translates to 4.8, well above what MLB starters typically allow, and a K-BB% that looks strong at AA but lands right at the MLB mean once adjusted. If the command tightens, he's a rotation starter with a genuine out pitch; if it doesn't, the walks eat the strikeouts and what's left is a depth arm hunting a role.

reports.name: Max Clark
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the lead. At AAA in 2026, Clark is punching out at 16% across 418 plate appearances — a number that translates to 18.7% against big-league pitching, well below a league average that sits around 22%. That's a contact profile you can build a lineup around, not a feel-good minor-league number propped up by inferior competition. The power is modest for now, a .157 ISO at AAA that translates to .134 against MLB arms, so the ceiling here is a patient, on-base-first center fielder with 21 stolen bases adding a wrinkle, not a middle-of-the-order bat. If the contact quality holds as pitching gets smarter, he's an everyday CF; if the pop doesn't develop past what it is right now, you're looking at a solid second-division regular who gets on base and runs.

reports.name: Luis Lara
reports.published_report: The contact and patience are loud: a .432 OBP at AAA, 54 walks against 48 strikeouts in 346 plate appearances, and a K% that translates to 17.6% at the MLB level while the average big-leaguer strikes out at 22.0%. Lara hits for average and gets on base at an elite clip, and the 24 stolen bases give him a real center-field offensive profile. The translation is honest about what he isn't, though: a .130 MLB-equivalent ISO tells you the game-to-game impact depends on contact and speed, not power, and if the BABIP softens when he faces better pitching, the ceiling lands closer to a low-end everyday regular than anything beyond it. That's the profile — a CF who earns his at-bats with a strike-zone approach that would play up immediately, but whose ceiling is ultimately capped by what the bat does when contact rates normalize.

reports.name: Hunter Goodman
reports.published_report: 16.7% barrel rate. That's the whole argument for Hunter Goodman, and it's a loud one — 98th percentile, sitting alongside the game's most dangerous power hitters by that measure. The xSLG of .467 and a projected .534 SLG over 540 plate appearances tell you the raw thump is translating, even in a sample that includes road games. What doesn't fit is the contact profile: a 33.0% strikeout rate and a 40.4% chase rate that rank near the bottom of the league drag his xBA down to .231, which is why the xwOBA of .329 reads modest despite the barrel numbers. If pitchers learn to exploit that chase tendency more consistently, the home run total shrinks fast and what's left is a catcher who swings and misses a lot; if the barrels keep coming at this rate in a full season, 39 home runs from behind the plate is a genuinely rare season.

reports.name: Riley Greene
reports.published_report: A 14.6% barrel rate with a 12.4% walk rate is a legitimately dangerous offensive profile, and the .363 xwOBA says the underlying quality of contact is well ahead of what his actual slash has shown Detroit fans. The tension in Greene's profile is straightforward: he barrels the ball at a rate that puts him in genuine company, he draws walks, he doesn't chase at an alarming rate, but 27.0% strikeouts bleed enough value that his xBA sits at .258 even when his xSLG is .478. If that strikeout rate drifts lower, the power and patience combination cashes into something approaching a true middle-of-the-order bat. At its current level, he's a .269/.359/.452 producer, a very good everyday outfielder who leaves real production in the batter's box.

If the command tightens and the walks come down, you can see a back-end starter; if the 4.4 stays where it is, he's organizational depth at the next level.

reports.name: Seth Hernandez
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest thing on the page, and the walk rate is the thing you have to watch. Across A+ & A in 2026, Seth Hernandez has struck out 118 batters in 74 innings, 14.3 per nine, with a K-BB% of 30 that sits in the 99th percentile of his pool, and a 2.4 ERA with a 1.1 WHIP. Translated to a major-league context, that strikeout rate softens to something around league average, and the walk rate, 3.8 per nine in the minors translating to 4.0, is the honest ceiling tax: if the command doesn't sharpen, the swing-and-miss isn't enough to carry a rotation spot. Back-end starter if it comes together; depth arm if it doesn't.

reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is almost uniformly ugly, and the projection follows it there. An xwOBA of .271 sits at the 3rd percentile of the league, xBA at .224, xSLG at .330 — contact quality that has no business belonging to a guy projected for 22 home runs. reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it doesn't fully survive the translation. At AAA in 2026, Williams has drawn 47 walks across 359 plate appearances, a 13% clip that maps to 10.8% in an MLB context, still above a league that walks at 8.5%, but his strikeout rate translates to 23.1% against that same league's 22.0%, and his ISO lands at .131 against a .15 MLB average, meaning the discipline shows up in the numbers but the power isn't carrying its weight once the level adjusts. The whole profile hinges on whether the batting average, currently sitting at .233 AAA with a .282 BABIP, can stabilize enough at the big-league level to keep the OBP functional without the power to compensate when it doesn't. Either a fringy everyday regular if the contact improves, or a bench bat whose walks keep him employed.

reports.name: Wei-En Lin
reports.published_report: The WHIP is 1.0 across AAA & AA, and that's the most honest thing in this profile. Wei-En Lin is limiting baserunners at an elite clip for a 20-year-old, and his 17 walks in 53 innings translate to a 3.2 BB/9 at the MLB level, matching what an average big-league starter allows, which means the command is functional but not a separator. The strikeouts are the catch: 54 punchouts across AAA & AA sounds fine until the MLB translation comes back at 8.0 K/9, a tick below where the average MLB pitcher lands, and the whole profile hinges on whether he can generate more whiffs against better hitters than he's seeing now. If the contact management holds and the swing-and-miss ticks up, he becomes a multi-inning reliever with a useful K-BB%; if neither develops, you've got a depth arm who keeps the ball off the bases until the wrong hitter comes along.

reports.name: Max Meyer
reports.published_report: The 2614 rpm fastball spin is doing real work here. Meyer's whiff rate sits at 28.6% and his K% at 26.2%, both legitimately above the middle of the pack, and you can trace both back to that elite spin — it's not a shape you manufacture. The trouble is the contact quality when hitters do make contact: a 42.0% hard-hit rate and an 8.6% barrel rate that land in the bottom third of the league, which is why his xERA of 3.87 sits well north of the 2.80 ERA the projection carries. Walk rate at 8.9% is the quiet drag, barely below average, and if it firms up this year the strikeout-to-contact trade-off gets a lot friendlier. He's a solid mid-rotation starter when the command holds, and a depth arm churning innings if it doesn't.

reports.name: Brandon Sproat
reports.published_report: The fastball at 96.7 mph is the one thing working in Sproat's favor, and the Statcast profile makes clear how much is riding on it. His chase rate sits at 25.5%, which is about as low as it gets, and when hitters aren't chasing, an 11.6% walk rate is what you get. The strikeout rate at 24.2% is league-average territory, not bad, but his xERA of 4.85 and a hard-hit rate of 43.1% say he's not missing barrels consistently enough to survive contact. If he ever finds a secondary offering that generates genuine swing-and-miss outside the zone, there's a functional back-end starter here; without it, the arm speed points toward a bullpen role and not much else.

reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is loud, the command is the problem, and right now the problem is winning. Across 61.7 innings at A+, he's punched out 73 hitters at 10.7 K/9, but 51 walks at 7.4 BB/9 have produced a 1.8 WHIP and a 6.70 ERA that leaves almost no argument for the present. Two innings. That's the honest anchor for everything that follows here — 2.0 IP at AA is a whisper, not a read, and the translation reflects it with low confidence attached to every number.

reports.name: Brady Smith
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and the translation is where it gets complicated. Across A+ & A, Brady Smith is punching out hitters at 13.2 per nine over 80.7 innings, 118 strikeouts against 34 walks, and that K-BB% sits in the 94th percentile of the pitcher pool. The problem is that when you run the MLB-equivalent translation, the strikeouts flatten to 8.7 per nine, essentially league average, and the walks translate to 4.2 against a translated K-BB% of 13.1 percent where the MLB average sits at 13.5, meaning the dominant shape at the lower levels becomes a break-even profile one level at a time. The whole case hinges on whether the swing-and-miss travels up the ladder or belongs to the level.

reports.name: Hector Osorio
reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile. Across A+ & A, Hector Osorio has walked 54 times against just 50 strikeouts in 394 plate appearances, a combination that translates to an 18.4% strikeout rate at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.
